title: $10M histotripsy research center launches to advance sound wave-based cancer treatment
description: Expanding use of a noninvasive, ultrasound-based cancer treatment is the ultimate goal of the new University of Michigan Histotripsy Center, a first-of-its-kind facility launched today.
body: Key takeaways
Expanding use of a noninvasive, ultrasound-based cancer treatment is the ultimate goal of the new University of Michigan Histotripsy Center, a first-of-its-kind facility launched today.

Invented at University of Michigan Engineering, histotripsy is the first commercially available ultrasound-based approach to treating tumors, allowing them to be destroyed without surgery and with few side effects to patients. Since receiving FDA authorization for liver tumors in 2023, U-M startup HistoSonics has installed over 130 treatment systems around the world, and they’ve been used to treat over 5,000 patients.

The Histotripsy Center is open for use by researchers both inside and outside U-M. The broader access to its specialized equipment and unparalleled, inventor-level expertise is expected to accelerate the technology’s scientific and clinical progress and enable more patients to benefit faster.

“Michigan is at its best when our brightest minds connect to tackle the most consequential challenges facing society,” said U-M President Domenico Grasso. “We see that today in the Histotripsy Center.

“Decades from now, I believe histotripsy will be spoken of alongside U-M’s historic contributions to the polio and influenza vaccines, and the many other discoveries that have defined our university’s commitment to improving and saving lives.”
Support to establish the $10 million center came from multiple sources including HistoSonics, Michigan Engineering, the Li Ka Shing Foundation and other private donors.
A center for research and education
Initially, the histotripsy research center will take a three-pronged approach to bolstering research and education.
Phase two of the center will focus on training clinicians who explore new treatment indications and push promising new human trials forward.
Broadening access to histotripsy testing equipment and expertise

The center’s strategy is to make collaboration with outside institutions as easy as possible. Researchers can come to Ann Arbor to perform tests with the center’s equipment—which is not commercially available, said Zhen Xu, the Li Ka Shing Professor of Biomedical Engineering, a professor of radiology and neurosurgery, and a co-inventor of histotripsy.
For researchers who cannot come to Ann Arbor, a histotripsy “travel system” of U-M’s machines and experts can travel to locations around the U.S. free of charge.

“In the next half decade, I envision the Histotripsy Center expanding from our lab to support thousands of researchers around the country, conduct as many as 100 projects at one time, publish over 100 joint papers and file 50 patents a year,” Xu said. “Using this high research productivity as a solid foundation, we expect to see 3-5 new FDA approvals for new diseases and to be able to treat hundreds of thousands of patients in the next five years.”
A treatment for tumors and more

Histotripsy treatment targets tumors with highly precise sound waves, causing the gases within cancerous cells to create bubble clouds. The repeated expansion and collapse of those clouds breaks apart the tumor cell’s structure. All that remains is a liquid that is eventually passed out of the body.
What sets histotripsy apart is its ability to destroy tumors without the physical and emotional toll that comes with surgeries, chemotherapy and radiation.

“The future of cancer care will be defined not only by greater precision and effectiveness, but by our ability to fundamentally reimagine the patient experience,” said Thomas Wang, dean of the University of Michigan Medical School and chief academic officer at Michigan Medicine. “Histotripsy represents a remarkable step toward that future, offering an innovative, noninvasive approach to treating tumors while opening the door to entirely new possibilities in cancer care.

“What makes the Histotripsy Center particularly significant is its ability to bring innovation, clinical care and discovery together under one roof. Through rigorous research and collaboration, we can better understand the potential of histotripsy, refine its applications, and explore how this technology might evolve into new approaches to treating cancer and other complex conditions. The discoveries made here could help shape entirely new paradigms of care.”
Bringing histotripsy to the world

In 2009, a small group of U-M engineers and doctors founded HistoSonics to commercialize histotripsy technology. Fourteen years later, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration approved histotripsy for treating liver tumors.
FDA authorization is expected for kidney and pancreas tumors in the next year. A new clinical trial for prostate hyperplasia is currently enrolling patients.

“The opening of the new center at U-M represents an exciting next chapter in the evolution of this groundbreaking science,” said Mike Blue, HistoSonics’ president and CEO. “It will play an important role in continuing to advance the technology, allow us to explore new applications with the potential to radically change the standard of care across many significant diseases, and ultimately unlock the full potential of histotripsy for patients around the world.”
In June, HistoSonics reached a valuation of $3.75 billion and now employs roughly 500 people, with offices in Ann Arbor and corporate headquarters in Minnesota.
Xu and the University of Michigan have a financial interest in HistoSonics.

title: 30 years of impact: U-M unites global leaders to advance nursing
description: The University of Michigan School of Nursing welcomed 20 nurse leaders, educators, policymakers and healthcare stakeholders from 10 countries across Latin America, the Caribbean, Asia and the Pacific for a weeklong program focused on advancing nurse practitioner education through shared learning, co
body: The University of Michigan School of Nursing welcomed 20 nurse leaders, educators, policymakers and healthcare stakeholders from 10 countries across Latin America, the Caribbean, Asia and the Pacific for a weeklong program focused on advancing nurse practitioner education through shared learning, collaboration and global partnership.

The immersive program, “Developing Advanced Practice Nurses Globally,” explored nurse practitioner education, practice, leadership, legislation and political engagement through presentations, discussions and collaborative learning.
The program also launched the U-M School of Nursing’s celebration of the Office of Global Affairs’ 30th anniversary, highlighting three decades of global partnerships and impact.

During the week, the School of Nursing hosted a signing ceremony for a memorandum of understanding between U-M and the Universidade Federal do Amazonas. The agreement further strengthens the institutions’ shared commitment to planetary health and sustainability.
“A defining strength of this program is its deep commitment to mutual learning, respect and collaboration,” said Jeanne-Marie Stacciarini, U-M School of Nursing associate dean for global affairs.

“While our guests came to explore the development of nurse practitioner education, our faculty, students, staff and community partners also benefited from learning how countries around the world are addressing their own health challenges. Those conversations strengthen all of us and create lasting partnerships that extend far beyond a single week.”

Throughout the week, participants shared expertise across the full spectrum of advanced practice nursing. Sessions explored curriculum development, clinical education, simulation, leadership, health policy, global competencies and community-based care. Visits to community health organizations and Michigan Medicine gave participants firsthand insight into nurse practitioner practice in a variety of settings.

“Participating in this program has been a truly transformative experience, broadening my perspective and reinforcing my belief that investing in advanced practice nursing means investing in better health outcomes for the population,” said Ludimila Cunha, a member of the Brazilian Federal Council of Nursing.

“I will return to Brazil inspired by the possibilities of innovation, leadership and professional autonomy, committed to fostering dialogue and advancing initiatives that will help shape the future of nursing.”

Although each participant brought a perspective shaped by their country’s healthcare system, a common theme emerged throughout the week: advancing nurse practitioner education requires both local leadership and global collaboration.

“It has been a tremendously valuable professional experience to learn from the experts and leaders in advanced practice nursing at U-M,” said Juana Mercedes Gutiérrez Valverde of the Autonomous University of Nuevo León in Monterrey, Mexico.

“The program strengthened my perspective on nursing leadership and provided practical knowledge and recommendations that will guide my work to further advanced practice nursing in Mexico. While we have made important progress, we are still in the early stages of developing advanced practice nursing. The need for this education is both clear and urgent.”

The exchange of ideas and experiences throughout the week underscored the value of global collaboration in advancing nursing education and practice. The shared lessons are at the heart of the U-M School of Nursing’s international partnerships and its ongoing commitment to preparing nurses to address health challenges worldwide.
The new agreement with the UFAM further reflects that commitment, creating opportunities for collaboration around planetary health, nursing education and shared global priorities.

“For 30 years, global engagement has been central to how the U-M School of Nursing advances health for all,” Webel said. “Bringing together nurse leaders from around the world reflects our commitment to learning with and from one another, building meaningful partnerships and preparing nurses to care, create and lead in every community they serve. These exchanges of ideas strengthen our global community and challenge all of us to think differently about how we educate nurses and improve health.”

“Many of the most pressing health challenges of our time extend beyond geographic boundaries and require shared solutions. Programs like this create opportunities for nursing leaders to exchange knowledge, adapt successful approaches to local contexts and accelerate innovation. When we learn from one another across countries and health systems, we expand our collective capacity to improve health and well-being in communities around the world.”

title: 9/11 at 25: U-M experts can discuss
description: University of Michigan experts are available to talk about a range of issues related to the 9/11 terror attacks and the quarter century since.
body: EXPERTS ADVISORY
University of Michigan experts are available to talk about a range of issues related to the 9/11 terror attacks and the quarter century since.

Javed Ali, associate professor of practice at the Ford School of Public Policy, began teaching in 2018. His government career in Washington, D.C., spanned from 2002-18, where he held positions in the Defense Intelligence Agency and the Department of Homeland Security before joining the FBI.

Before his government career started, he was in Washington on the morning of the attacks, and passed the Pentagon about 30 minutes before the third hijacked plane hit the building. A few minutes later, he could see the smoke rising from the Pentagon in the aftermath of the attack.

Based on his experience in Washington and the additional insights he’s developed since teaching at U-M, he’s had time to reflect on what the attacks meant for the country. He says one of the most important developments was “the government’s ability to degrade and disrupt the abilities of terror groups from directly attacking the U.S.—at least at the scale and impact of 9/11—driven by new laws, tools and capabilities.”

On the other side of the spectrum, he says, “the post-9/11 era created ethical and moral dilemmas associated with mass surveillance measures, detention and interrogation programs, and military operations that put hundreds of thousands of U.S. troops in harm’s way and killed or wounded civilians and noncombatants. In addition, the direct financial costs of the wars in Iraq and Afghanistan totalled in the trillions of dollars, according to some estimates.”
Event: 25 years after 9/11: Reflections on the U.S. war on terror
Contact: alimust@umich.edu
Juan Cole, professor of history at the College of Literature, Science, and the Arts, studies the ongoing political change in the Middle East.

“Twenty-five years after the Sept. 11 attacks, the United States is still mired in the Middle East, this time in a war with Iran, a country that held candlelight vigils for the U.S. in 2001, since its Shiite Muslim population had also been targeted by al-Qaeda,” he said. “America’s debt has ballooned from its expenditure of trillions of dollars on unnecessary wars. The U.S. political class cynically blamed Iraq for 9/11, leading to an 18-year quagmire in that country that helped create new al-Qaeda offshoots such as ISIL.

“Tens of thousands of veterans suffer from war injuries or PTSD and suffer high suicide rates. Police departments that received excess war materiel became distant from their own communities and often seemed like occupation forces themselves.
“The wars and occupations manifestly failed, diminishing U.S. standing in the world.”
Contact: jrcole@umich.edu

Mike Barger is a clinical assistant professor of business administration at the Ross School of Business and former executive director of Ross Online. His resume includes a 13-year career in the U.S. Navy as a pilot, flight instructor and, ultimately, chief instructor at the Navy Fighter Weapons School (commonly called TOPGUN). He left the Navy to be a founding member of JetBlue Airways and created JetBlue University, the company’s centralized training department.

“Twenty-five years later, I still think first about the people who lost their lives, the families changed forever and the extraordinary courage shown on Sept. 11th and in the days that followed,” he said. “From a leadership perspective, 9/11 also taught me something I have carried ever since: A crisis begins affecting people long before leaders fully understand what is happening.

“At JetBlue that morning, we had emergency plans, but no playbook for the world we suddenly entered. We still had to make consequential decisions with incomplete information, care for our customers and crewmembers, collaborate with our industry colleagues and regulatory partners—all while learning and adapting as events unfolded. That experience now shapes how I study and teach crisis leadership at Michigan Ross.

“Leadership in turbulent times is not about the elimination of uncertainty. It means taking action before the path forward is perfectly clear, while remaining ready to adjust as understanding improves. It is the disciplined work of creating clarity, confidence and forward momentum for others while never losing sight of the people who are living with the devastating consequences of the crisis.”
Contact: mgbarger@umich.edu

Michelle Kees, clinical associate professor of psychiatry at the Medical School, is the faculty lead for the Eisenberg Family Depression Center’s outreach and education initiatives, including a program named in honor of Todd Ouida, a young U-M alumnus who lost his life on 9/11 after overcoming anxiety disorders in childhood.

“The Ouida family transformed the unimaginable loss of their son, Todd, on 9/11 into an extraordinary legacy of hope for children and families,” she said. “For more than two decades, their support has helped us advance research, clinical care, and education in child mental health, while keeping Todd’s story and his experience with anxiety at the heart of this work. Their generosity has touched generations of clinicians, researchers, and, most importantly, the children and families we serve.”

As a child psychologist whose own work was funded by one of the first Ouida awards two decades ago, Kees says that the 9/11 anniversary presents a special challenge and opportunity to young people and their parents.

“For children and teens who are encountering 9/11 for the first time, it’s important to remember that they may experience the events very differently than adults who lived through them. Parents can help by limiting repeated exposure to graphic or frightening images, checking in about what their children are seeing and hearing, and creating space for questions and conversations.
“It’s also OK to share your own memories, keeping in mind that children benefit most when those conversations leave them with a sense of safety, connection and reassurance about the present.”
Contact: Kara Gavin, kegavin@umich.edu

Yasmin Moll is an associate professor of anthropology at the College of Literature, Science, and the Arts. She is an expert on religion, media and politics in the Middle East and the author of “The Revolution Within: Islamic Media and the Struggle for a New Egypt.”

“With rising social polarization, misinformation and the normalization of Islamophobia in American media across the political spectrum, the tragic memory of 9/11 is being weaponized to target, delegitimize and even criminalize Muslim-American civil rights organizations, social justice activists, elected officials and ordinary people,” she said.
Contact: ymoll@umich.edu

title: A quarter century later, landmark U-M study revisits Black health and aging
description: Twenty-five years after launching the nation's largest representative survey of Black Americans' health, University of Michigan researchers will reconnect with as many as 7,000 original participants to investigate aging, dementia risk and changes in their communities.
body: RESEARCH TO WATCH

Twenty-five years after launching the nation’s largest representative survey of Black Americans’ health, University of Michigan researchers will reconnect with as many as 7,000 original participants to investigate aging, dementia risk and changes in their communities.

The follow-up to the National Survey of American Life (2001-03) will create a rare, decades-long longitudinal dataset, allowing researchers to examine how participants’ health, communities and experiences have changed since the original interviews. They want to understand aging as a lifelong process and why Black Americans face a two-to-four-times higher risk of dementia compared to other groups.

“This research will provide the data we need to create policies, institutions and programs that benefit the American public,” said Toni Antonucci, U-M professor of psychology and research scientist at the Institute for Social Research. “Our participants’ shared experiences of life, health and community will become part of an incredible scientific resource.”
The new wave adds cognitive testing, physical measurements and an optional blood draw to help researchers examine biological risk factors associated with dementia.

“Our goal is to understand how to reduce the burden of dementia in America,” said Briana Mezuk, U-M professor of epidemiology and co-principal investigator. “To do that, we are focusing on a group that has elevated risk of this condition. If we can understand the factors that are driving this elevated risk, we can translate that into interventions that address them.”
This initiative will begin in Michigan before expanding nationwide.

“As the study grows, one of its strengths is its multidisciplinary team,” said Courtney Thomas Tobin, co-principal investigator and UCLA associate professor of community health sciences. “We bring together researchers from six institutions with expertise in epidemiology, psychology, sociology, community health, gerontology, neuroscience and community-based participatory research.”
Researchers will mail letters to former National Survey of American Life participants during the last week of August. Interviewers will begin calling in September to schedule appointments.

The late James S. Jackson, one of the nation’s foremost social scientists, led the original NSAL. Jackson was a former director of both the Program for Research on Black Americans and U-M’s Research Center for Group Dynamics, where the NSAL is housed. The study remains one of the most frequently cited datasets on the health of middle-aged and older Americans.

“The NSAL 25-year follow-up builds on Dr. Jackson’s legacy of groundbreaking research, including his earlier National Survey of Black Americans launched in 1979 that provided the first representative view of Black America,” said Deborah Robinson, ISR assistant research scientist and project director. “Many of the researchers involved in the current follow-up learned from and were inspired by his mentorship.”

Previous research using NSAL data has examined how older adults seek help, how parental education affects children, how families and faith communities provide support, what we know about suicidal behaviors among teens, and what activities can help with depression.

“Hearing from these same survey participants after 25 years gives us a window into how life paths unfold, how challenges and opportunities shaped health, and how communities have changed over time,” said NSAL postdoctoral fellow Eskira Kahsay. “Each participant brings experiences that cannot be replaced and together they reflect the lives of thousands of Black Americans across the country.”

Researchers will reach out to past participants by phone and mail to invite them to join the follow-up study. They can earn up to $150 while helping answer key questions to improve Americans’ health and well-being.
The NSAL is funded by a grant from the National Institutes of Health, 1R01AG087121-01A1.

title: Abuse and disability trap: 90% of incarcerated Michigan youth suffered prior abuse
description: Nearly every incarcerated male youth in a new University of Michigan study experienced some form of prior physical abuse.
body: Study: The Comorbidity of Violence Exposure, Mental Health, Cognitive Functioning, and Disabilities in Incarcerated Youth (DOI: 10.1007/s40653-026-00960-w)
Nearly every incarcerated male youth in a new University of Michigan study experienced some form of prior physical abuse.

Nine in 10 were exposed to at least mild physical abuse, one-third suffered severe prior sexual abuse, and two-thirds reported adverse childhood experiences, according to U-M researchers, who looked at incarcerated adolescents ages 13-20 at a single all-male juvenile detention facility in Michigan.

“What really stuck out to me most was the sexual abuse rate, that 70% of them had at least some exposure to sexual abuse,” said Suzanne Perkins, research assistant professor at the U-M Institute for Social Research. “I’ve worked with a lot of kids, so very few things upset me in the work that I do. But when I saw that statistic, I just burst into tears. I couldn’t believe that it was such a high statistic.”

According to the study, published in the Journal of Child & Adolescent Trauma, 85% of the teenagers had a learning disability, a mental health condition or both. More than 75% showed signs of a learning or cognitive disability during direct testing.

The findings also showed that more than 60% had a disability listed in their official records before the study. In addition, 80% met the criteria for multiple diagnoses and 25% qualified for five or more diagnoses.

“Children with genetic disorders or disabilities are much more likely to be targeted for violence and sexual abuse,” Perkins said. “At the same time, violence causes cognitive problems through brain injury mechanisms. The relationship is bidirectional.”

Perkins and colleagues reviewed medical and educational records, surveyed participants about their experiences with violence and trauma, and also conducted individual cognitive and educational testing.

According to the researchers, the relationship between disability and violence can work in both directions. Young people with disabilities may be more vulnerable to abuse, while violence and trauma can contribute to cognitive problems.
The study also highlights the importance of identifying learning and cognitive problems early.
“Schooling is really central,” Perkins said. “Young people who have missed school or struggled academically may need interventions for reading, attention, organization and planning.”
The study suggests that support should address the broader circumstances surrounding young people’s lives, including housing, food, healthcare and dental care.
“It’s a multipronged problem that really requires social work and schools and counseling, and not just policing,” Perkins said.

The study also included cognitive experiments testing inhibition and other executive functions—direct testing that Perkins said is less common in research on incarcerated youth, which tends to rely on medical and educational records.
The findings suggest that understanding these kids’ learning and cognitive needs could help schools and service providers identify problems before they become harder to treat.
“If you want to stop this from being an ongoing problem, you really need to start with early intervention,” Perkins said.

title: Advancing clean energy equitably
description: With support from the Alfred P. Sloan Foundation, researchers from the University of Michigan and Michigan State University are examining who benefits from a city's sustainability efforts and who has a say in them. In addition to faculty and students, the project's collaborators also include communi
body: WHAT’S THE STUDY: With support from the Alfred P. Sloan Foundation, researchers from the University of Michigan and Michigan State University are examining who benefits from a city’s sustainability efforts and who has a say in them. In addition to faculty and students, the project’s collaborators also include community partners who are studying six different initiatives to advance clean energy technology deployment, reduce carbon emissions and increase energy affordability in Detroit, Chicago and Columbus.

WHY IT MATTERS: Cities nationwide are investing billions of dollars in clean energy and climate infrastructure, yet there aren’t conclusive answers to how and whether these projects pay off for the residents living closest to them. This grant will use these case studies to learn how to better ensure that residents have a voice in efforts to decarbonize their cities and are sharing in the benefits of these projects.
HOW MUCH AND FOR HOW LONG: The $1 million collaboration is funded for three years.
WHO’S INVOLVED:

Tony Reames, the Tishman Professor of Environmental Justice at the School for Environment and Sustainability, or SEAS, founded the Urban Energy Justice Lab and Energy Equity Project. He directs the U-M SEAS Detroit Sustainability Clinic and served as deputy director for energy justice and principal deputy director for state and community energy programs at the U.S. Department of Energy in the Biden administration.

“This project gives us a unique opportunity to understand how residents participate in planning processes, how benefits and burdens are distributed, and how local governance shapes project outcomes,” he said. “Those insights will help us better understand what it takes to advance energy transitions that are not only effective but also equitable.”

Meghan Wilson, assistant professor of American politics and public policy at Michigan State University, researches issues at the intersection of public policy, urban development and race. She analyzes critical questions about how public institutions, and those influenced by them, imagine themselves in the future.

“This project puts residents’ experiences at the center of how we define success,” she said. “What sets it apart is that we are not just measuring outcomes, we are centering the people living through and shaping these transitions with partners like Blacks in Green, the city of Detroit, IMPACT Community Action and American Addition.”

title: AI outperformed humans in a prediction tournament featuring technology ventures
description: For decades, the idea that artificial intelligence can beat humans at number-crunching tasks like high-frequency trading has been widely accepted.
body: Study: The strategic foresight of LLMs: Evidence from a fully prospective venture tournament (DOI: 10.48550/arXiv.2602.01684)
For decades, the idea that artificial intelligence can beat humans at number-crunching tasks like high-frequency trading has been widely accepted.
But strategic foresight—the ability to predict the success of high-stakes, uncertain business ventures—has long been held as a uniquely human superpower.

A study co-authored by a University of Michigan business expert suggests artificial intelligence is beginning to surpass human prediction capabilities in the context of predicting the success of new ventures.

“Strategy felt so different from algorithmic trading,” said Felipe Csaszar, a professor of strategy at U-M’s Ross School of Business. “It was, in a sense, obvious that algorithmic trading was doable, because it was all about numbers. But strategy is all about words.”
The findings could mean businesses no longer need to compete on once rare, specialized strategic forecasting skills, but how they integrate AI-generated predictions.

According to Csaszar, the frontier of AI possibilities in the field of strategy has shifted significantly. To test this theory, he and his co-authors, Aticus Peterson of New York University and Daniel Wilde of Indiana University, conducted a prospective prediction tournament using 30 live crowdfunding projects. These technology ventures were launched after the training cutoffs of the AI models studied, ensuring the models could not use past data in their evaluations.

Various large language models completed 870 pairwise comparisons, producing rankings of predicted fundraising success. These forecasts were benchmarked against the predictions of 346 managers and three investors trained in MBA programs.

In this specific scenario, top-tier LLMs were significantly more accurate than the human experts. While the best human results correctly identified a winner in 3 out of 5 comparisons, the top-performing model, Gemini 2.5 Pro, achieved a correlation of 0.74—correctly identifying the winner in nearly four out of five cases.

The research identified a phenomenon dubbed the “augmentation trap,” where combining human and AI judgments actually reduced overall accuracy compared to the AI working alone. The addition of human judgment introduces idiosyncratic noise and error that degrades the final result.
“In this case, the wisdom-of-the-crowd logic doesn’t produce an improvement in accuracy,” Csaszar said. “If you include a human in the mix, performance decreases.”
Csaszar explained AI’s success stems from its ability to overcome human’s “bounded rationality”—the inherent cognitive limits humans face regarding time, memory and consistency.
“AI is very promising because it relaxes some of these bounds,” Csaszar said. “No human has read as much as ChatGPT; no human has as much time to think about each project.”

The study also suggests a model’s success is related to its performance on Humanity’s Last Exam, one of the most difficult benchmarks, which measures AI’s graduate-level knowledge on a broad range of subjects.
“The ability to predict what’s going to happen requires a broad set of knowledge that you get from knowing about multiple fields and being able to (reason) about those,” Csaszar said.
This suggests strategic foresight depends on a model’s ability to connect disparate concepts across domains rather than simple pattern matching or data retrieval.

AI’s progress in this research may appear to mirror the 1997 “Deep Blue” moment in chess, which proved that machines could master tasks once thought to require human intuition. However, Csaszar says that while chess has world champions like Garry Kasparov to beat, strategic foresight lacks a clearly identified top-tier competitor to serve as a benchmark.
Because the experiment was limited to a specific setting, Csaszar said, “We are not saying that the ‘chess moment’ has arrived, but it does appear that what AI can do in strategy has changed.”

Just as the Industrial Revolution lowered the cost of physical labor and the internet lowered the cost of information, Csaszar noted AI could lower the cost of the high-level reasoning required for strategy.

He says when the cost of cognition drops, it changes what defines a company’s “competitive advantage.” If the ability to predict the future (foresight) is no longer an expensive, rare human skill but an accessible AI output, firms will have to compete on other things, such as how they integrate those predictions or what unique data they own.
“Cognition is everywhere, so this will have effects everywhere,” he said.

title: America at 250: What still unites us
description: Turn on the television, scroll through social media or listen to political commentary, and it's easy to conclude that America has never been more divided. Yet beneath the headlines and heated debates lies a different story: one of shared beliefs, common values and surprising agreement.
body: EXPERT Q&A

Turn on the television, scroll through social media or listen to political commentary, and it’s easy to conclude that America has never been more divided. Yet beneath the headlines and heated debates lies a different story: one of shared beliefs, common values and surprising agreement.

As the nation marks its 250th anniversary, sociologist Wayne Baker, professor emeritus of organizational behavior and human resource management, says Americans have far more in common than many realize.

Drawing on years of research, Baker found that people across political, religious, geographic and demographic lines continue to share fundamental values, and even agree on hundreds of public policy issues. In this Q&A, he explains why July 4 became America’s Independence Day, what his research reveals about common ground, and why understanding our shared values may be more important than ever.

Many Americans associate July 4 with the Declaration of Independence, but most delegates actually signed the document on Aug. 2, 1776. Why do you think that part of the story has largely been forgotten, and what can it teach us about America’s founding?

Declaration was a process. Several dates could qualify as the “official” date of American independence. July 2, 1776, was the date when the Continental Congress voted to approve the resolution that declared independence. John Adams, then a congressional delegate from Massachusetts, thought that July 2 would become the date Americans celebrated. Congress formally approved the written Declaration on July 4 and it was signed by the delegates on Aug. 2, 1776. And a case could be made that September 3, 1783, is the best official date, because that’s when Britain signed the Treaty of Paris and formally recognized the independence of their former colonies.

July 4, 1776, is the date printed on the Declaration of Independence and distributed to the general public. That’s why we celebrate the 4th of July as the official date of independence. I wouldn’t say the story has been forgotten per se as much as it’s been simplified. The process of independence—the grievances, various proposals of independence and all the steps taken—is taught in our schools. We may not remember the details of our civics classes, but we do remember the main result, and the 4th seems like the best official date for the reason stated above.
What are the values that consistently unite people across political, demographic and geographic differences?

Using data from four representative surveys of the American people, I identified 10 values that are “core” in the sense that they are widely shared among Americans, strongly held, stable over time, and supported across political, religious, regional and demographic differences. Here are five:
If Americans agree on many fundamental values and even on more public policies than many assume, why does the perception of deep division remain so strong?

The perception of a deep division is the result of a confluence of factors. At the most basic level, it’s human nature to think of the world in dual opposites: day and night, heaven and earth, land and sea, and so on. Add to that the tendency for Americans to view political and social issues as morality battles between good and evil. Add to that the psychology of group polarization. And, of course, there’s social media, which exaggerates our differences, and politicians who benefit by fanning the flames of division and discord.
Why do you believe focusing on our shared values matters now more than ever?

What holds together a nation as large and as vast as America? Each person knows or meets a tiny fraction of the population. So, what holds us together is a belief of a common ideology, a sense of solidarity and belonging to the same people. This “imagined community” is threatened by the pervasive rhetoric of division. So, I hope that the findings from my research will remind people that yes, indeed, we do have a lot in common, including 10 core values and agreement on hundreds of policy proposals.

In everyday life, this means pausing to consider that the next person you meet is likely to share a lot with you, even if outward appearances suggest otherwise. It means starting with the assumption of good intentions and common ground. It means giving the other person the benefit of the doubt. And, if you find differences, to explore them with a sense of curiosity and willingness to understand.

title: Arts taking center stage at U-M throughout October
description: Football season. Back to school. The fall can be a busy time of year. But the arts are planting their flag in the month of October, too.
body: Football season. Back to school. The fall can be a busy time of year. But the arts are planting their flag in the month of October, too.
Through the Michigan Arts Festival, kicking off its second year on Oct. 1, the University of Michigan is showcasing myriad arts experiences available to the U-M community.

With over 300 student organizations, more than a dozen galleries and exhibition spaces, a packed performance schedule from the School of Music, Theatre & Dance and beyond, new exhibits at the U-M Museum of Art and other campus museums, there is no shortage of inspiration to be found. The month-long festival is a small snapshot of the endless arts opportunities open to the U-M community all year long.

“The World Health Organization has scoped 3,000+ studies that show how the arts are good for individuals and good for social connection,” said Mark Clague, executive director of the U-M Arts Initiative. “Today, when trust and social connection are so fragile and funding for the arts is increasingly hard to find, participating in the arts may be more important than ever.”
The festival takes an active role in the university’s efforts to create more connection and address the prevalent issues of social isolation and anxiety that so many college students face.

The newly minted ArtsRx program for social prescribing combines forces between University Health & Counseling, Wolverine Wellness, Student Life, School of Music, Theatre & Dance, Stamps School of Art & Design, UMMA and the University Musical Society. Now, UHC can prescribe an arts program created by the ArtsRx team to supplement their clinical work with a patient, and take further steps toward improved mental health. The first prescription Arts Meetups are available now, with two taking place during the festival.

With many free and low pressure options, the festival wrangles what might otherwise be an overwhelming maze of programming and instead serves as a guide to discover the right arts experience for an individual’s schedule and interests.
With a slate of meaningful programming, some highlights include:

“The arts at Michigan are truly world class and are found everywhere from UMMA and the stage of Hill Auditorium to the classroom,” Clague said. “The big message is that the arts are part of what makes the University of Michigan great, and that you can’t get the full campus experience without giving the arts a try, too.”

title: Back to school: U-M experts can discuss a range of topics
description: University of Michigan experts are available to comment on critical topics facing schools this academic year. Their areas of expertise include student mental health, concussions, school safety, AI in the classroom, recovery from learning loss, teacher retention, Black girls' schooling experiences, s
body: EXPERTS ADVISORY

University of Michigan experts are available to comment on critical topics facing schools this academic year. Their areas of expertise include student mental health, concussions, school safety, AI in the classroom, recovery from learning loss, teacher retention, Black girls’ schooling experiences, school meal funding, immigration, and college campus speech and protest.
Literacy, challenges and opportunities for schools, educators and students

Elizabeth Birr Moje is the dean of the Marsal Family School of Education and the George Herbert Mead Collegiate Professor of Education. Her research examines young people’s culture, identity and literacy learning in and out of school in Detroit, where she leads Marsal Education’s participation in the Marygrove Learning Community, a Detroit P-20 Partnership. Moje also directs the Michigan Education Teaching School on the Marygrove campus.
Moje can comment on adolescent literacy, effective teaching and the science of reading. Her research covers teacher preparation, shortages, edtech, education justice and student wellness.
Contact: fpires@umich.edu
Jean Mrachko is the associate director of Michigan Alternate Route to Certification, an accelerated certification-only teacher preparation program at the Marsal Family School of Education.
Contact: jmrachko@umich.edu

Chris Torres, associate professor of educational policy and leadership at the Marsal Family School of Education, can discuss how state policies and the K-12 school budget might affect teacher recruitment and retention, and how and why districts might be differentially impacted by new policies.
Contact: chtorres@umich.edu

Samantha Keppler, the NBD Bancorp Assistant Professor of Technology and Operations at the Ross School of Business, is an expert in education operations. Her recent projects examine how districts purchase supplies (and the million-dollar price tag when teachers take time to get supplies on their own), how they implement cell phone bans (trade-offs between lockers, pouches or off-versus-away rules), and how they are training teachers on AI tools (it shouldn’t be to speed up or automate work).

“Michigan now has an instructional time cell phone ban, and this year districts need to make a plan: Buy cell phone lockers, pouches or simply adopt ‘off and away’ rules,” she said. “Running the numbers, lockers are going to be feasible only in small schools. Pouches relieve the teacher burden of constant phone monitoring at low cost, and would be what I would recommend—especially for middle schools.”
Contact: srmeyer@umich.edu
Teaching practice

Deborah Loewenberg Ball is the Jessie Jean Storey-Fry Distinguished University Professor of Education at the Marsal Family School of Education, research professor at the U-M Institute for Research and director of TeachingWorks. She researches elementary math teaching as a tool to build student agency and combat educational inequity. Amid national debates and new state legislation on PK-12 math instruction, she can comment on math education controversies, effective teaching practices and teacher preparation.
Contact: dball@umich.edu

Angela Calabrese Barton is the Alvin Demar Loving Sr. Collegiate Professor of Education and chair of educational studies at the Marsal Family School of Education. She studies how science and engineering learning can better engage young people in schools, after-school programs and community settings. Her research examines how educators, youth, families and community partners can work together to design STEM learning experiences that are meaningful, relevant and connected to issues that matter in students’ and families’ lives.
Calabrese Barton can discuss how educators and schools can expand meaningful STEM learning opportunities for young people, particularly those historically marginalized in education and society.
Contact: fpires@umich.edu

Alaina Neal-Jackson is a clinical assistant professor at the Marsal Family School of Education. Her research focuses on Black girls’ schooling experiences, school discipline and the school-to-prison pipeline, restorative justice in education and the policies and practices that shape educational equity. She is also the co-founder of The REACH Center, a school-based restorative justice center.

“The reality is that if we do not address the challenges educators face in translating restorative justice into everyday practice, we will see school communities wanting to turn to the next thing,” she said. “But what comes after restorative justice and the commitments it represents? Are they commitments that encourage us to consider the conditions that give rise to harm, to prioritize respect for students’ humanity and to work toward healing above all? If we believe these commitments are worth preserving, our focus must shift to working more intentionally to support educators to fully embrace restorative practices within their pedagogy and everyday interactions with youth.”
Contact: alainamn@umich.edu
Higher ed

Demetri Morgan is an associate professor of education in the Center for the Study of Postsecondary and Higher Education at the Marsal Family School of Education. He co-directs the Center for Strategic & Inclusive Governance. His research examines how governance and student political engagement shape institutional change in higher education.

Morgan can help reporters connect back-to-school stories to the larger questions colleges face about campus speech, protest, institutional purpose and public trust. He can speak to how governing boards and campus leaders can respond to conflict without losing sight of learning, academic freedom and their responsibilities to students and the public.
Contact: dlmorg@umich.edu
Instructional practices with technology

Liz Kolb, clinical professor of education technologies at the Marsal Family School of Education, can address how teachers can continue using what they learned during remote and hybrid learning to teach online.
Contact: elikeren@umich.edu

Rebecca Quintana is an associate professor of education practice at the Marsal Family School of Education. Her research explores how emerging technologies shape learning design and instructional practices. She can discuss educational applications of generative AI, learning experience design, online learning and immersive learning environments.
Contact: rebeccaq@umich.edu
Adjustments for children

Pamela Davis-Kean is a professor of psychology at the College of Literature, Science, and the Arts and director of the Survey Research Center at the Institute for Social Research. She has examined the various pathways that the socioeconomic status of parents relates to the cognitive achievement outcomes (particularly mathematics) of their children. To help students navigate the pandemic’s impact on lower achievement scores, she recommends starting mentoring programs and creating individualized education plans for each student.
Contact: pdakean@umich.edu

Sandra Graham-Bermann, professor emerita of psychology at the College of Literature, Science, and the Arts, can discuss how parents can help their children cope with stress/time management as they return to school.

“Kids come back to school carrying a variety of experiences, some wonderful and some that might be related to living in an unstable household with some kind of trauma,” she said. “Teachers would do well to understand children’s behavior from a trauma-focused lens to best assist those that need help.”
Contact: sandragb@umich.edu
Health and wellness

Matthew Boulton is the Pearl L. Kendrick Collegiate Professor of Global Health and professor of epidemiology and preventive medicine. His research interests are in global health, global vaccine equity, childhood vaccinations and vaccine preventable diseases, preventive medicine, and infectious disease epidemiology in low- and middle-income countries.
Contact: mboulton@umich.edu

Rebecca Hasson is the Victor L. Katch Collegiate Professor of Kinesiology and director of the Childhood Disparities Research Lab at the School of Kinesiology. She can discuss ways to promote physical activity both inside and outside of the classroom.
Contact: hassonr@umich.edu

Laura Gultekin, clinical assistant professor at the School of Nursing, has spent the past several years partnering with community agencies to improve the well-being of families experiencing homelessness.
Contact: lgulteki@med.umich.edu

Laura Richardson is a clinical associate professor of applied exercise science and movement science at the School of Kinesiology. Her expertise focuses on using behavior modification strategies and exercise to help treat a wide array of health conditions.
Contact: laurari@umich.edu

Steven Broglio, director of the Michigan Concussion Center and professor at the School of Kinesiology, currently serves as the president of the international Concussion in Sport Group. He can discuss concussion research and prevention and concussion in sports.
Contact: broglio@umich.edu

William Lopez, clinical associate professor of health behavior and health equity at the School of Public Health, specializes in the effects of immigration policies and the health impacts of law enforcement on individuals. This school year, he says, brings heightened concerns and fears as federal law enforcement forces increase deportations.
Contact: wdlopez@umich.edu

Kate Bauer is a professor of nutritional sciences at the School of Public Health and co-director of the Institute for Food, Nutrition & Health Policy. Her expertise touches on SNAP benefits, school meals and other nutritional aid for people struggling to afford food.

“As of last month, about 1 million children across the U.S. have lost access to SNAP. Nearly all of the children who have lost SNAP are eligible for the program; the problem is that the states are struggling to keep up with all the administrative changes and families are not able to reach their caseworkers, paperwork is getting lost, etc. so these families are dropped. Without SNAP, these kids may not automatically qualify for school meals and with fewer kids automatically qualifying, some school districts are not able to offer school meals for all through the Community Eligibility Provision.”
Here in Michigan, she pointed out, the state is continuing its support of Healthy School Meals for All again this coming year.

“This is a huge blessing for all families who now don’t have to put time and money into making sure their children can eat during the school day,” she said. “Food prices are also up from this time last year and many food pantries can’t keep up with the increased demand that they’re experiencing. Overall, families are really stressed and worried, and we’re not getting much clear guidance from the federal or state governments about what’s going to happen with food assistance over the next year.”
Contact: kwbauer@umich.edu

Anand Parekh is a board-certified internal medicine physician, chief health policy officer at the School of Public Health and former deputy health secretary for the U.S. Health and Human Services. He can speak to decreasing vaccination rates and an all-time high vaccine exemption rate for kindergartners as the U.S. experiences its worst year for measles cases in 35 years.

“The decision to skip vaccines appears to often be based on inaccurate information and puts millions of schoolchildren at risk of serious preventable illnesses,” he said. “It also endangers communities, especially the most vulnerable among us, the elderly and the very young. We are seeing vaccine-related policy decisions at the federal level that cause confusion and fear and seem to be more politically motivated than focused on preventing the spread of contagious disease. The political climate sadly is leading parents to make decisions that they may falsely believe are in the best interest of their children but are leading to sickness, death and suffering.

“While there can be valid reasons for exemptions to vaccines and there is respect for the right of parents to vaccinate or not, it cannot be said often enough that vaccines are safe and effective and the best bet at keeping a child healthy and strong. Not vaccinating is a gamble with their health and the public’s health, a gamble that more and more often is backfiring and senselessly, needlessly leading to serious illness and death. I hope parents will trust that the best way to keep their children healthy is to vaccinate.”
Contact: akparekh@umich.edu

Emily Martin, professor of epidemiology at the School of Public Health, is co-director of the Michigan Center for Respiratory Virus Research and Response and the Michigan Public Health Integrated Center for Outbreak Analytics and Modeling. She can speak to contagious disease trends, vaccines, vaccine waiver requests, and what parents and schools need to know to best protect students, teachers and families.
Contact: etmartin@umich.edu

Sara Adar, professor of epidemiology at the School of Public Health, and Meredith Pedde, assistant research scientist in epidemiology at the School of Public Health, have researched the benefits of replacing diesel-fuel-powered school buses with electric ones. They can share their findings and knowledge on differences in academic achievement and absenteeism between students who ride gas-powered buses vs. electric-powered vehicles. Their research revolves around an ongoing U.S. Environmental Protection Agency rebate program that randomly awards funding to school districts to replace old buses with cleaner models that produce less pollution.
Contact: sadar@umich.edu and mpedde@umich.edu
School safety

Justin Heinze is an associate professor of health behavior and health equity at the School of Public Health and director of the School Safety section at the Institute for Firearm Injury Prevention. He is also principal investigator of the annual Healthy Minds Study and director of the National Center for School Safety. He can discuss a range of school safety and student mental health topics and can explain the recommendations in a recent national report on the impact of active shooter drills on student health and well-being.
Contact: jheinze@umich.edu
Sarah Stilwell, research investigator at the Institute for Firearm Injury Prevention, can discuss aspects of student and school safety outside of firearm violence prevention.
Contact: stillwel@umich.edu

Elyse Thulin, research assistant professor at the Institute for Firearm Injury Prevention, can discuss school safety, technology, confidential reporting systems, social media and school violence risks, bullying, suicide and mental health concerns.
Contact: ethulin@umich.edu

title: Beyond hunger: Food insecurity in later life linked to dementia
description: Older adults who experienced food insecurity in both midlife and later life had nearly four times the risk of probable dementia as those who remained food secure, according to new University of Michigan research.
body: Study: Associations between mid-life and later-life food insecurity on probable dementia in a national sample of United States adults (DOI: 10.1016/j.ajcnut.2026.101386)

Older adults who experienced food insecurity in both midlife and later life had nearly four times the risk of probable dementia as those who remained food secure, according to new University of Michigan research.

The study, published in The American Journal of Clinical Nutrition, found the strongest association among people experiencing food insecurity later in life. Researchers found no significant association between food insecurity in midlife alone and probable dementia.
Food insecurity is often discussed in terms of hunger and access to adequate nutrition, but researchers increasingly are examining its potential connections to health across the life course.

The study used longitudinal data from the Institute for Social Research Panel Study of Income Dynamics, the longest-running nationally representative household panel survey in the United States. The survey allowed researchers to track food insecurity within the same families over decades and examine whether the timing of food insecurity was associated with cognitive health in later years.

“Not only can we now track the changes one family experiences, but by collecting this information for decades, we can also examine different parts of the life course,” said Noura Insolera, assistant research scientist at ISR. “We have known for some time that hunger and nutritional deficiencies make it harder for children to learn in school, for example, but only by collecting this information year after year for many years can we look at something like the connections between food insecurity and dementia risk.”

This study followed 2,051 adults and looked at whether they experienced food insecurity at two different periods: midlife (1999–2003) and later life (2015–2019). Of the total of the adults studied, 3% experienced food insecurity only in midlife, 5.2% experienced it only in later life and 5% experienced it during both periods.

While food-insecure families are in the minority, when it occurred mattered. The association with probable dementia was concentrated among those who experienced food insecurity in later life, rather than midlife alone.

The findings suggest that food insecurity in later adulthood may be particularly important to cognitive health. However, the study cannot determine whether food insecurity itself contributes to dementia or whether other factors associated with food insecurity help explain the relationship.

“Food insecurity has different adverse impacts across the life course,” Insolera said. “If you have been to the doctor recently, there are often screening questions for food security upon intake, but health practitioners are often at a loss when tasked with helping their patients. They are often not equipped, as medical doctors, to solve these problems. The first step is identifying the problem by asking questions, but the next step is much more complicated.”

The people who experienced food insecurity in both midlife and later have an estimated probability of dementia of 40% as compared with 11% of those who were food secure in both midlife and later life. Those who reported food insecurity in later-life only also saw a statistically significant increased probability of 34%.

“As individuals age, there are many factors, including financial safety, community, family and government programs that help to make sure needs are met,” Insolera said. “If someone is forced to choose to pay a bill that may accrue interest if unpaid or spend less money on food, the food is often seen as the easier option to forgo.

“The physical toll that a lack of nutrition has on the body is a tangible health issue, but the mental strain of worry and anxiety about where their next meal might come from is also a very real problem. Food insecurity causes both of these, and the combination of these adverse physical and mental conditions can create a problem that is larger than the sum of its parts.”
The findings also raise questions about how health care providers and policymakers can respond to food insecurity, researchers said.

“If there is one thing I could change, it would be to go back to the generosity of benefits that SNAP was able to provide during the pandemic,” Insolera said. “The federal government was able to swiftly intervene and help American families in a very successful way. If those levels of benefit would have been kept, we might not see the increases in food insecurity we have seen since those benefits expired.”

title: Beyond India-Pakistan: What the Mecca defense pact reveals about a changing security order
description: The new defense agreement bringing together Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Türkiye adds another layer to an increasingly complex security landscape stretching from South Asia to the Middle East.
body: EXPERT Q&A
The new defense agreement bringing together Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Türkiye adds another layer to an increasingly complex security landscape stretching from South Asia to the Middle East.

The Mecca agreement establishes a collective-defense framework among three countries with significant military capabilities but very different strategic relationships. Türkiye is a NATO member, Saudi Arabia is a longtime U.S. security partner, while Pakistan maintains deep ties with China. For India, the agreement is noteworthy because of its longstanding tensions with Pakistan and its own growing strategic relationships with the United States and Gulf countries.

Javed Ali, associate professor of practice at the University of Michigan’s Gerald R. Ford School of Public Policy and a longtime national security practitioner, discusses what the agreement could mean for India, Pakistan and the wider region, and why the relatively restrained responses from both New Delhi and Washington are worth watching.
What does this agreement change for India and its security relationship with Pakistan?

It is still too early to know exactly how the Modi government is viewing this development. India has not come out strongly in opposition to it, but given the longstanding tensions between India and Pakistan, I have to imagine New Delhi is taking note. Whether it presents a greater security risk to India is less clear. It appears to be a defensive security coalition among three very different countries that do not share borders but are influential in their respective spheres.

What I think is also important is the broader trajectory of Pakistan. Over the past couple of years, Pakistan has made headway in raising its profile on the world stage, including in its dealings with the Trump administration and its involvement in regional conflicts and diplomatic efforts. Its role around the Iran conflict, for example, has been notable. The Mecca agreement seems to fit into that broader pattern. So from India’s perspective, this may not be about an immediate or direct threat to its security. It is also about Pakistan expanding its diplomatic and security profile in ways that India will be watching closely.
Pakistan has deep ties with China. Does the agreement risk creating a wider China-aligned security axis that could put additional pressure on India?

Maybe, but I would be cautious about making that connection. China already has deep commercial and economic ties in the Gulf, particularly because of its reliance on energy from the region. But for the most part, China has not projected military power into the Gulf in the way the United States has. Its influence there has been more political and economic. India is likely looking at this and asking whether the agreement somehow gives China an additional strategic advantage. Maybe it does; maybe it does not. I don’t think we know that yet.

This is almost like three-dimensional chess being played across the region. A move involving Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Türkiye is going to be interpreted not only by those three countries, but also in New Delhi, Beijing and Washington. At this stage, however, I would not characterize this as a China-aligned security axis encircling India.
If the agreement is not primarily about India or China, what is driving it?

One way to understand it is in the context of Iran and the broader security environment in the Middle East. Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Türkiye are three Muslim-majority countries with very different ethnic, cultural and strategic backgrounds. They also come into this agreement with different security relationships; Türkiye through NATO, Saudi Arabia through its Gulf and U.S. relationships, and Pakistan through its own relationships, including with China.

But there could be a shared interest in strengthening their ability to respond to threats in the region. I think the agreement can be viewed, at least in part, through the lens of the broader effort to counter the Iranian threat. That interpretation could also help explain why we have not seen strong public opposition from Washington. From the U.S. perspective, this could be seen as another piece of a broader regional security architecture rather than an arrangement aimed at India.
So, Türkiye is a NATO member; Saudi Arabia is closely tied to the United States and Pakistan has a deep relationship with China. What happens if those commitments collide during a crisis?

That is one of the serious questions that will have to be worked out. If Türkiye becomes involved in a conflict under this three-country agreement, for example, what does that mean for its NATO commitments? Would that trigger any NATO Article 5 obligations? Why would countries such as Germany, France or Spain necessarily come to Türkiye’s aid in a conflict that does not directly affect NATO or mainland Europe?

I have to imagine these kinds of questions were considered before the agreement was put into place and that there is some understanding of how those obligations would interact. More broadly, each country had to ask what it gains from joining this coalition, what resources it may have to contribute, and what obligations it assumes if a conflict affects one of the other members. In some ways, this is International Relations 101. Countries maintain overlapping relationships because each one is trying to maximize its own interests. The real test comes when those relationships create competing obligations.
Does the agreement tell us something larger about how countries are responding to uncertainty over America’s role in global security?

It may. This could partly reflect a perception that the United States is not necessarily going to be the guarantor of its allies’ security in the way it has been in the past. Creating another security arrangement is one way for countries to minimize some of that risk. All three countries have significant military capabilities. They may not individually have capabilities at the level of the United States, but each brings considerable personnel, resources, money and/or military capacity. Operating under a broader umbrella potentially gives them another mechanism for responding to threats.
You pointed to Washington’s relatively muted response as particularly interesting. Why?

I think the absence of strong public U.S. opposition is an interesting signal in and of itself. This agreement does not directly obligate the United States to do anything. But the United States has important relationships with all three countries, and Türkiye is a NATO member. I would have to imagine that if the Trump administration strongly opposed this agreement, it could have put pressure on these countries not to move forward. That does not appear to have happened publicly.

We also haven’t seen the kind of strong reaction from the administration that can make its opposition to an international development very clear. That raises the possibility that the United States was aware of where these negotiations were going and perhaps had some level of tacit acceptance. I want to be clear that this is an assumption on my part—we don’t know what happened behind closed doors. But if Washington had been surprised or strongly opposed, I think we might have expected a different public response.
New Delhi has also been relatively restrained. What does the silence from both India and the United States tell us?

That parallel is interesting. The United States increasingly sees India as a key regional player, and the U.S.-India relationship has grown at the economic, military and political levels. Washington has little incentive to deliberately make an enemy out of India or take actions that overtly antagonize New Delhi and disrupt that broader relationship.

So, if the perception in India were that this agreement was somehow designed by Washington to contain or encircle India, I think that would be an incorrect way to understand how the United States views India. The fact that neither the Indian government nor the U.S. government has strongly criticized the agreement could indicate that there was considerable discussion behind the scenes, or at least that both governments had some awareness of what was developing.

Again, that is an assumption. We don’t know what those conversations looked like. But governments assess the second- and third-order consequences of developments like this. If both Washington and New Delhi remain publicly restrained, that is something worth paying attention to.
What should India be watching now?

For India, I think the important thing is to watch what this agreement actually becomes rather than assume from the outset that it represents a hostile bloc. Pakistan’s growing international profile will certainly be important to New Delhi. So will the possibility of closer security coordination among Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Türkiye. India will also be watching how China views the arrangement and whether Beijing’s role changes.

But there is a larger story here as well. The security architecture across South Asia and the Middle East is becoming more complicated. Countries that have very different relationships with Washington, Beijing and each other are increasingly building overlapping partnerships rather than fitting neatly into one geopolitical camp. The Mecca agreement may be another indication of that shift. What matters next is how these commitments work in practice, particularly when one of these countries faces a real security crisis.

title: Beyond the 'Great Divide': What we really know about political polarization
description: Americans are deeply divided. At least that's what we've been told for years. But how divided are we really? A new review suggests the answer may depend on how researchers ask the question.
body: Study abstract: Measuring affective polarization: Matching concepts to measures (10.1111/pops.70152)
Americans are deeply divided. At least that’s what we’ve been told for years. But how divided are we really? A new review suggests the answer may depend on how researchers ask the question.

The analysis involving University of Michigan experts argues that researchers need to take a closer look at who Americans are thinking about, what they are being asked, and the political circumstances surrounding the question before concluding how polarized the country is.

For nearly 15 years, scholars have measured the emotional distance between Democrats and Republicans—what researchers call affective polarization. Yet there is still no single way to measure it, and seemingly small choices about a survey can produce dramatically different pictures of how much Americans dislike the other side.Measuring the “Great Divide” is more complicated than asking Americans whether they like or dislike the other party.

“Researchers must consider who people have in mind—is it politicians or is it everyday voters—when they are answering questions about polarization,” said Yanna Krupnikov, U-M professor of communication and media. “And the size of the gap between feelings toward their own party and the opposing side.”
Using data from the American National Election Studies at U-M’s Institute for Social Research, the analysis highlighted several findings:
The data on which party is more polarized is inconclusive and inconsistent, said John Barry Ryan, U-M associate professor of political science and of communication and media.
“Across different studies, not just this analysis, and data sources, it is not clear that one side is more polarized than the other side,” he said.

The study, which appeared in Advances in Political Psychology, was co-authored by lead author James Druckman, University of Rochester; Samara Klar, University of Arizona; and Matthew Levendusky, University of Pennsylvania.

title: Beyond the park boundary: When green space has polluted neighbors
description: More than half of U.S. public parks are within two miles of an active industrial facility that handles toxic chemicals, according to a new University of Michigan study.
body: Study: Proximity of parks to polluting sites in the United States (DOI: 10.1038/s41598-026-65808-7)
More than half of U.S. public parks are within two miles of an active industrial facility that handles toxic chemicals, according to a new University of Michigan study.

About 80,000 such parks are listed on the federal Toxics Release Inventory. In addition, nearly 27,000 parks are close to a toxic waste site requiring emergency federal cleanup, known as a Superfund site. Of those parks, more than 2,400 contain land that directly overlaps with a Superfund site.

Using data from ParkServe, U-M researchers cross-referenced an inventory of 151,366 public parks with the locations of TRI facilities and Superfund sites. The park inventory included everything from national and state parks to local hiking trails and school playgrounds available for public use.
The results, published in the journal Scientific Reports, show that green spaces and industrial or hazardous waste sites frequently overlap or are located near one another across the United States.

“We wanted to inform the public about the many interlocking features that make up our neighborhoods and communities,” said co-author Elliott Chemberlin, a scholar in the Junior Professional Researcher program at the Institute for Social Research. “While spaces like parks are easy to spot, polluting sites often hide in plain sight—even right next to where we live and work. We aimed to show how these dynamic, overlapping uses of space shape a more nuanced portrait of the neighborhood environment.”

The study, partly funded by the National Institutes of Health, identified 63 parks with Toxics Release Inventory facilities inside their boundaries and more than 14,000 parks with such facilities within half a mile.

The researchers created a web map and public dataset to help communities identify where parks, TRI facilities and Superfund sites overlap or are located near one another. The information is available through the National Neighborhood Data Archive.

“While communities may experience health benefits from parks, our findings indicate that this does not necessarily occur in isolation from toxic exposures,” said Philippa Clarke, U-M professor of epidemiology and ISR researcher. “Understanding that parks and polluting sites overlap adds important nuance to public health research on the health benefits of green space.”

Studies show that public parks can improve health by encouraging exercise, supporting mental well-being and strengthening communities. Park trees also improve air quality, lower neighborhood temperatures and increase property values.

Research also has linked living near industrial facilities or hazardous waste sites to increased health risks, including higher rates of heart and lung disease, cancer, birth defects and neurological disorders.
The study did not measure pollution inside parks or assess whether park users were exposed to pollutants.

“Determining how much exposure to pollution might occur in any given park depends on many factors that our study did not measure, such as the types and concentrations of pollutants present; whether pollutants are concentrated in soil, water or air; how well they are contained and managed; what remediation efforts have taken place; and even weather patterns that determine how pollutants disperse and travel,” Chemberlin said.
The findings can help communities, policymakers and researchers identify locations where additional testing, analysis or advocacy may be warranted.

“We can use the mapping tool to identify polluting sites that may be operating in and around our parks,” Chemberlin said. “It can be a starting point for more research into how those sites could be affecting parks and communities. We hope communities and officials also use this tool to support advocacy related to public-space use and urban planning.”
How parks and industrial sites became neighbors

Historically, city parks and factories were built side by side along waterways, while national parks in the West were sometimes established near mines, according to the study. Today, some former industrial sites and landfills are remediated and redeveloped as public parks.

“Many parks are deliberately built on previously contaminated land after it has been ‘remediated,'” Clarke said. “Making these data available to the public can help urban planners identify land farther from polluting sites when considering where to construct new parks.”
Co-authors of the study also include ISR researchers Robert Melendez, Kate Duchowny, Lindsay Gypin and Grace Noppert.

title: Bird-friendly mural takes flight at U-M's Weiser Hall
description: A student-designed bird-friendly window mural will soon transform the elevated walkway connecting Weiser Hall and the North University Building, part of a broader effort to reduce bird collisions and support biodiversity at the University of Michigan.
body: A student-designed bird-friendly window mural will soon transform the elevated walkway connecting Weiser Hall and the North University Building, part of a broader effort to reduce bird collisions and support biodiversity at the University of Michigan.

Suher Salim, an undergraduate student studying cognitive science in the College of Literature, Science, and the Arts, created the winning design, which features birds, butterflies and botanical elements woven through an intricate black-and-white pattern. The design will be installed in white film across the glass walkway, helping birds recognize the glass as a barrier.

“The inspiration for the design came from everyday nature I encountered while walking in Ann Arbor. I wanted to specifically feature native plants to bring awareness on campus. As an artist, it is really surreal to have an art installation on the U-M campus,” Salim said. “I believe we must learn to coexist with nature, because we are also a part of it.”
Salim also holds an associate’s degree in graphic design from Oakland Community College and said that training helped her plan a design that could work as a large-scale installation.

The winning design was selected through a campuswide competition launched earlier this year as part of U-M’s Bird Protection Program. Funded through Student Life’s Planet Blue Student Innovation Fund, the competition invited students to create an original mural-style decal that met bird-friendly design standards while adding artwork to the campus landscape.

The competition was hosted by the Office of Campus Sustainability and Innovation in partnership with the Arts Initiative and the College of Literature, Science, and the Arts. A jury reviewed the submissions and selected Salim’s design.
